Orthopedics · published research

Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction

In a randomized trial, pain and function improved after both low-level laser and orthotic insoles; insoles performed better at nine months, and neither approach produced a clinically important strength gain.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a randomized trial, pain and function improved after both low-level laser and orthotic insoles; insoles performed better at nine months, and neither approach produced a clinically important strength gain.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tendons > Tibial tendon category contains one unique human randomized controlled trial with 52 participants who had stage-two posterior tibial tendon dysfunction. No other direct clinical publication, animal study, or laboratory record was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Participants were randomly assigned to low-level laser therapy or insoles. Both groups improved in foot pain and function after treatment. At nine months, the insole group had better values, and neither treatment had a clinically important effect on muscle strength (Koltak and Yurt 2021). The study compares two active approaches rather than laser with sham or no treatment, so it does not establish how much of the improvement came from laser itself or from recovery and concurrent care.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal evidence was identified for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction in the exact category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 850-nm near-infrared laser at 100 mW, with reported point energies ranging from about 0.7 to 7 J across the treated sites. Fourteen sessions were delivered over five weeks. The comparison group received orthotic insoles. The database does not identify the source country, so none is assigned.

Interpretation

The trial supports improvement over time in both groups but does not show laser superiority to insoles. Follow-up suggests that orthotic treatment may be more effective for longer-term pain and function in this sample.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain and function change in a randomized comparison with orthotic insoles Very low for superiority over orthoses or durable strength improvement
Publications and records1 unique title in the exact category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The only direct study randomized 52 people with stage-two posterior tibial tendon dysfunction to laser or insoles, but it did not include sham or untreated control. Both groups improved after treatment, and insoles had better values at nine months. Further trials against sham and usual care would clarify absolute treatment effects.

Publication and study types

  • Human RCT1 (52 participants; randomized comparison with insoles)
